newsitem.title: USA: Consumer group criticizes FDA's new mad cow rule.
newsitem.headline: Consumer group criticizes FDA's new mad cow rule.

text.p: A new Food and Drug Administration rule banning manufacturers from using the remains of most mammals to make animal feed doesn't go far enough to protect the public from mad cow disease, an influential consumer group said on Tuesday.
The rule, announced earlier Tuesday by the agency, should not exempt the remains of pigs from the ban, Consumers Union said.

"By failing to include swine in the rule, FDA has left the door open for a mad cow-like disease to circulate in the United States," said Michael Hansen, a food safety researcher for group that publishes "Consumer Reports" magazine.

The FDA said it exempted pig remains from the new rule because no cases have been reported of mad cow disease or related strains of the disease occurring in swine. But Hansen said that British scientists showed that pigs could get the disease when injected with brain material from an infected cow.

"FDA claims we are safe because we have never seen swine infected under natural conditions," Hansen said. "But it could just mean we have not looked hard enough. Most commercial pigs are slaughtered at the age of six months, long before they would be expected to exhibit any signs of the disease."
Pig remains left on the slaughterhouse floor constitute about 16 percent of all rendered mammal protein used in farm animal feed, Consumers Union said.
The FDA rule becomes effective in August and is designed as an additional safety measure since mad cow disease broke out in Britain in 1986.
Scientists believe that the disease was rapidly spread there by the practice of feeding animal byproducts to cows.
No case of the deadly nervous system disease, known to scientists as bovine spongiform encephalopathy, has been found in the United States.
The new FDA regulation forbids manufacturers from grinding up carcasses, spinal cords or other leftover parts of most mammals to make feed for cows, sheep and goats.
The U.S. government banned British beef exports in 1989, and some 17 human deaths in Britain and France have been blamed on the disease.
